terms.gloss: know (a fact); know how to (with an infinitive)
evidence: Varr. RR 2.1.2: nēmō enim omnia potest scīre
terms.comment: Facts: with an object, an accusative and infinitive, or an indirect question (scīre quid agās). With an infinitive, know how to (vincere scīs); of a language, scīre Latīnē (Cic. Brut. 140, Lewis & Short). Quod sciam, as far as I know (Cic. Att. 16.2.4). People and places one knows take nōvī instead.

terms.gloss: not know; Nesciō, I don’t know
terms.comment: The ordinary way to say it: nōn scīre is rare, and Cicero says it already sounds barbarous beside nescīre (Or. 157, cited by Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: phrase: the person informed in the accusative; dē and the ablative, an accusative and infinitive, or an indirect question
evidence: Cic. Att. 3.11.1: faciam tē certiōrem quid ēgerim
terms.comment: The prose way to say “inform” (Lewis & Short, s.v. certus). In a letter, “let me know” is fac sciam or fac ut sciam.

evidence: Cic. Att. 5.19: fīliolam tuam et amō et amābilem esse certō sciō (Lewis & Short), s.v. amābilis
Ter. Eun. 5.2.50: volet, certō sciō (Lewis & Short), s.v. ah

terms.grammar: relative clause of restriction, with the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Fin. 2.7: (Epicūrus) sē ūnus, quod sciam, sapientem profitērī est ausus (Lewis & Short s.v. quī)
terms.comment: Traupman 115 has quoad ego sciō; the classical idiom is quod sciam, with the subjunctive. Quoad is “as long as, until”, and “as far as” only in phrases like quoad ejus fierī poterit.
Not found in the classical authors, who say quod sciam (above).

phrases.latin: vincere scīs, Hannibal; victōriā ūtī nescīs
phrases.english: you know how to win, Hannibal; you don’t know how to use a victory
let me know how you are
none, as far as I know

phrases.latin: pater, quī Bulgaricē nōn minus quam Latīnē scit
phrases.english: Dad, who knows Bulgarian no less than Latin
phrases.source: Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum

phrases.english: Do you know how to fish?
